newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu prepares for Zaire talks but rebels grumble.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu prepares for Zaire talks but rebels grumble.

text.p: Ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko of Zaire prepared for his first face-to-face encounter with rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Thursday but there were rumbles of discontent in the rebel camp about the U.S.-brokered arrangements.
Aides said Mobutu would fly to Gabon on Thursday before the planned meeting with Kabila on a South African navy ship in international waters in the Atlantic on Friday.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson told reporters in Kinshasa there were no preconditions for the talks, due to be chaired by President Nelson Mandela of South Africa.
But at rebel headquarters in Lubumbashi, south-east Zaire, officials told Reuters Kabila had not softened his position that Mobutu must accept his 32-year reign was over.
The officials said Kabila was surprised by Richardson's announcement in Kinshasa that "several African leaders" would attend the talks on the supply ship SAS Outeniqua.
The rebels do not want the talks with Mobutu to turn into a mini-summit about one of Africa's biggest political shake-ups for decades.
President Bill Clinton's envoy has shuttled between Mobutu and Kabila to try to set up the meeting and broker a peaceful end to the conflict.
"This is an historic occasion that hopefully will lead to a peaceful transition in Zaire," Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said after his 100-minute meeting with Mobutu.
There was no indication Mobutu had agreed to step down.
Richardson did not persuade Kabila to accept a cease-fire ahead of the talks or make any commitment to accept a transitional government before elections.
These are the key components of a peace plan approved by the United Nations whose special envoy, Mohamed Sahnoun, will attend the talks at sea if they take place.

Kabila launched the rebellion in the east of Black Africa's biggest country last October. His fighters have made short shrift of Mobutu's ragged army and now stand poised to attack Kinshasa from their new forward base at Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) to the east.

Mobutu, debilitated by cancer and looking frail at his meeting with Richardson on Wednesday, is in effective control of a small area of Zaire's land mass. It includes the capital, the port of Matadi and a thin sliver of frontier leading to his home region around Gbadolite.
State radio said the traditional May Day parade would not be held in Kinshasa on Thursday because of the crisis.
The rebels grabbed Bumba, south of Gbadolite, with no resistance on Tuesday and were set to take Mobutu's nearby birth-place at Lisala, residents in radio contact with Kinshasa said.

In a sign of the growing fragility of his rule, Mobutu's military governor in Kinshasa said on Wednesday travellers crossing the Zaire river to neighbouring Congo would need a special permit, state media said.
The governor, General Amela Lokima, said the intention was to monitor movements "at this time of crisis".

The presidential camp views Richardson's mediation with some cynicism since it believes the United States plotted with African countries, led by Uganda and Rwanda, to end the Mobutu era. It dawned in 1965, ironically with total backing from the United States at a time Mobutu was seen in Washington as a key Third World bulwark against Communism.
